A 62-year-old man presented with double vision and a left facial droop. Neurological 
examination revealed binocular horizontal diplopia. Examination of the extraocular muscles at 
various points of gaze is shown in Figure 1a. On leftward gaze, he had an abduction deficit in 
the left eye and adduction deficit in the right eye. On rightward gaze, he had an adduction 
deficit in the left eye and nystagmus in the right eye. Upward gaze, downward gaze and 
primary position were unremarkable. He had difficulty closing his left eye with bell’s 
phenomenon seen and a marked facial droop (Figure 1b).  
 
This gentleman had one-and-a-half syndrome and left facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, or in short, 
eight-and-a-half syndrome. This is characterized by conjugate horizontal gaze palsy on 
looking to one side, internuclear opthalmoplegia on looking to the other side and unilateral 
facial weakness. The lesion is localized to the ipsilateral paramedian pontine reticular 
formation (PPRF), medical longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) and pontine tegmentum where the 
facial nerve nucleus resides. The PPRF, located anterior and lateral to the MLF, receives 
input from the frontal eye fields and plays a role in coordinating horizontal gaze. A lesion 
involving the PPRF causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy. The MLF is a fiber tract that 
originates from the abducens nucleus in the pons and extends to the contralateral oculomotor 
nucleus in the midbrain. A lesion involving the MLF results in failure of adduction of the 
ipsilateral eye and nystagmus of the contralateral eye on lateral gaze (internuclear 
opthalmoplegia).  
 
Eight-and-a-half syndrome is a rare neuro-opthalmologic syndrome that was first coined by 
Eggenberger.1 Close proximity of the PPRF, MLF and facial nerve nucleus in the dorsal pons 
make them vulnerable to demyelinating and vascular lesions. Various etiologies have been 
described, including ischemic strokes, multiple sclerosis and space occupying lesions.2, 3 This 
patient’s MRI showed an acute infarct in the left dorsal hemipons, consistent with his clinical 
findings. He was treated with aspirin and statins. He improved clinically and was 
subsequently discharged to a rehabilitation hospital.
